articles.title: Sophia, Study.com, or StraighterLine: which courses should you take first?
articles.description: Compare current subscription structures, course inclusion, assessments, and degree applicability so your first course purchase helps the degree you want to finish.
articles.lede: Choose the degree requirements before choosing the subscription. Sophia, Study.com, and StraighterLine can serve different parts of a plan. The useful starting provider is the one whose available courses fill your remaining requirements at a cost and pace that work for you.

sections.heading: Begin with the gaps in your degree plan
paragraphs: A provider can have a large catalog and a low monthly price without offering the particular course you need. Start with the receiving university, exact degree and format, and the requirements left after existing learning. Then compare the eligible course options for those rows.

This is especially important when several providers cover introductory subjects. If writing is already satisfied, another writing course may contribute nothing to the degree. If a course is accepted only as an elective and your elective space is full, the low purchase price does not make it a useful next step.

A provider’s ACE or NCCRS recommendation is part of its credit basis. It is separate from the receiving school’s decision to award credit and apply it to the degree. Keep the exact course identity, relevant recommendation dates, and receiving placement connected as you compare.

sections.heading: Compare the actual products being sold
paragraphs: The current Sophia profile lists a $99 monthly membership before applicable tax. Sophia ordinarily allows two active courses at a time, and written or project-based Touchstones can add grading time. Longer subscription products exist, but the monthly price alone does not establish your total.

Study.com’s current College Saver is listed at $95 per month, while College Saver Pro is $235. Course inclusion differs: Pro adds premium and upper-division options. The current plans advertise unlimited monthly completions with different concurrent-course limits. A study-help or test-preparation subscription is not the same as a credit-earning plan.

StraighterLine’s current profile lists a $99 monthly membership plus individual course charges. It also advertises selected-course packages with separate terms. Laboratory kits can add expense. Those structures should be compared with the exact courses in your basket rather than treated as one universal per-course rate.

sections.heading: Assessment style can change the right choice
paragraphs: Current Study.com support describes the required College Saver finals as open-book and non-proctored. Course-specific assignments still apply. That is a current product statement; older discussions describing a different exam model may no longer describe the product a student is buying.

StraighterLine’s current final Benchmark requirements use Honorlock, with a computer, Chrome extension, webcam identity check, and government ID. The exams remain open-book using authorized materials. Sophia uses Challenges, Milestones, and course-specific written or project work.

Look at the actual course and assessment requirements when a testing format matters to you. A self-paced course can still include monitored exams, essays, projects, laboratories, or grading delays. Selecting a provider with a comfortable format can be more useful than picking the lowest headline price.

sections.heading: Make the course basket before the calendar
paragraphs: Choose a group of courses that fill genuine open requirements. Identify prerequisites, projects, laboratory materials, and expected feedback steps. Then decide how many you can realistically work on during the paid period, using your available study time rather than someone else’s completion story.

A hypothetical $99 monthly subscription spread across three applicable courses in one paid month is $33 per course before tax or other charges. If the same three courses take two paid months, the membership share is $66 per course. These are arithmetic scenarios, not a claim that three courses can be completed in a particular period.

The most expensive result is often a paid course that does not help the target degree. Time spent selecting the right basket can prevent that result. It can also reveal when you should delay a subscription until prerequisites, materials, or a university evaluation are ready.

sections.heading: One degree can use more than one provider
paragraphs: Our reviewed WGU Business Management starting proposal uses both Sophia and Study.com options to assign 69 of its 110 competency units outside WGU. That example does not establish a universal provider order for every student. It shows why the destination-specific course map matters.

Another student may have college courses that replace many of those introductory requirements. A student whose destination accepts institutional coursework but little alternative credit may need a different source entirely. The plan should adapt to those facts rather than force every learner into the same brand sequence.

When comparing options, keep the receiving award separate from the source credit quantity. A WGU requirement worth four competency units can be met by a published source course whose original credit amount is different. Do not multiply a provider’s price by an assumed universal conversion.

sections.heading: Pick the first purchase with a clear purpose
paragraphs: Before paying, identify the requirement each selected course fills, confirm the product includes it, and decide when you can give the course attention. Read the current assessment and cancellation terms for that product. Keep the receipt and original course record with the rest of your learning information.

You can begin by browsing the course library without choosing a university immediately. Save courses that interest you, then compare their supported degree placements before starting them. If you already know your degree, use its mapped requirements to choose a smaller, more useful basket.

articles.title: My college won’t accept Sophia. What can I take instead?
articles.description: Explore self-paced university-issued credit from ASU Universal Learner, UMPI YourPace, and other sources when a destination requires institutional coursework.
articles.lede: A college that restricts Sophia or other alternative credit may still accept coursework taught and transcripted by an accredited university. ASU Universal Learner, UMPI YourPace, and individually taught university courses are different source types worth evaluating against the exact receiving degree.

sections.heading: Understand what the receiving school is asking for
paragraphs: ACE and NCCRS provide credit recommendations for designated learning. A receiving college decides what to accept and where it fits. University-issued coursework follows a different path: the institution that actually teaches and awards the course supplies the academic record.

That difference can open useful options for a student who wants a particular residential university or a program that limits alternative credit. It does not mean every university course transfers everywhere. The receiving equivalent, grade, credit quantity, laboratory format, and remaining degree requirement still matter.

Preserve the original source. A Sophia course later listed on a university transcript is still originally Sophia learning. It cannot inherit the receiving equivalency for a different course actually taught by that university. The opportunity is to take the appropriate institutional course, rather than change the label on earlier work.

sections.heading: ASU Universal Learner is one institutional route
paragraphs: ASU Universal Learner Courses let eligible learners take designated Arizona State University coursework and choose to purchase the academic credit after successful completion. The current published structure is $25 to enroll and $400 to add an eligible completed course to an ASU transcript, for $425 if converted.

The catalog includes session-based and on-demand options. On-demand does not mean there is no minimum participation period: the current profile identifies six weeks for three- or four-credit courses, four weeks for two credits, and two weeks for one. Assessment and proctoring requirements depend on the course.

Admitted degree-seeking ASU students are not eligible for this Universal Learner route under the current guidance. A student targeting another university also needs the receiving course placement; an ASU transcript by itself does not establish that the course fills a specific major or general-education requirement.

sections.heading: A subscription university can also supply individual courses
paragraphs: UMPI’s YourPace information describes nondegree course-taking as an option for eligible learners. That creates a different way to think about a competency-based institution: it can be a source of university-taught courses as well as the final destination for a degree.

For the 2026–27 pricing reviewed in the inventory, the undergraduate session is $1,800 for eight weeks. That charge belongs to the session rather than each course. If a student completes two applicable courses in one paid session, its tuition share is $900 per course; five would be $360 each. Those figures are pacing scenarios, not predictions of how many courses someone can complete.

YourPace generally serves applicants age 20 or older, with stated consideration for younger applicants who already hold an accredited associate or bachelor’s degree. The actual course list, prerequisites, and nondegree admission rules matter. Do not enroll in a whole session based on one appealing course title without a suitable receiving placement.

sections.heading: Other university-issued sources may fit particular gaps
paragraphs: Independent Study in Idaho includes courses issued by sponsoring institutions. The reviewed University of Idaho ENGL 3130 Business Writing and ENGL 3170 Technical Writing II examples each specify six projects, no exams, and at least 18 weeks. They illustrate why “self-paced” should not automatically receive a fastest-course label.

Portage Learning supplies another example, particularly for science and health prerequisites. Its current information identifies Geneva College or Bushnell University as the transcript issuer, depending on residence at registration. The published general rate is $230 per credit, with course and laboratory acceptance determined by the receiving program. Assessment requirements can include webcam-recorded exams.

A university transcript, a comfortable assessment format, a low price, and a short calendar are separate attributes. A course may match some of those preferences and not others. Select the combination that solves the requirement you actually need to complete.

sections.heading: Build a targeted institutional-credit basket
paragraphs: Start with the receiving university’s exact requirement and its published equivalency tools or agreements. Identify the original university course, not just the enrollment platform. Include the source course code, credits, required grade, prerequisites, delivery format, and the degree slot it is intended to fill.

This approach is especially useful for a small group of remaining requirements. A student might use a self-paced university source for writing, mathematics, or a particular prerequisite, then complete the major and campus experience at the final university. Another student may find a community-college articulation route more suitable.

Keep repeated or overlapping credits out of the total. Two writing alternatives that fill the same three-credit requirement are choices, not six applicable credits. Count a session fee once when several courses share it, and allow the calendar to reflect minimum participation and grading periods.

sections.heading: Keep the destination in view
paragraphs: For a campus route, choose a university the student actually wants to attend. Local access, an appealing campus, academic fit, and the desired experience should guide the search. An easy-to-document transfer relationship is useful when it serves that destination and the student’s goals.

DegreeSteps’s credit-source library separates institutional coursework from alternative-credit recommendations and examinations. Use those distinctions to explore suitable options, then connect each proposed course to a specific receiving requirement. A restriction on one credit source does not need to end the search for a practical route.

authors.name: DegreeSteps editorial team
authors.bio: We explain educational choices using university catalogs, receiving-school course agreements, provider guidance, and the same researched degree models used by DegreeSteps. Our articles distinguish proposed coursework, original learning records, and individual university awards. Worked examples identify their program, format, units, and relevant dates. Founder stories are attributed as reported experience, without invented transcripts, savings totals, or reviewer credentials.
